title: Mobile Bay dredging debate continues as Army Corps defends annual project - NewsBreak
text:
By Kate Sherman ,
1 hours ago
MOBILE, Ala. ( WKRG ) — The annual dredging of Mobile Bay is once again fueling debate between the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers and environmental advocates over how sediment should be managed.
How Daphne firefighters protect community through extreme summer heat wave WKRG News 5 got an exclusive look from the water as a massive bucket dredge removed sediment from the shipping channel, work the Corps says is critical to keeping the Port of Mobile open.
The dredge arrived in Mobile Bay about two weeks ago and is expected to remain for roughly seven months.
According to Colonel Kelcey R. Shaw, commander and district engineer for the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers Mobile District, the amount of sediment removed each year is enormous.
“600,000,000yd³. Measure four football fields each Football field 750 tall. So, the RSA building that’s in Mobile, four of those. That’s how much we removed every year,” said Colonel Shaw.
Shaw said maintaining the channel is essential for Alabama’s economy.
“We will lose the larger ships. We will lose the larger commercial port activity. If we were to stop doing this,” said Colonel Shaw.
Charges dropped against 16-year-old arrested in connection with fatal Pensacola shooting Cade Kistler with Mobile Baykeeper does not oppose the dredging itself, but where he says some of that sediment is ending up
“A lot of people who are seeing the effects on their shoreline, their property value, their livelihood, ability to see, clear water more often,” said Kistler.
Kistler said excess sediment can affect seagrass, oyster reefs, and other marine habitats.
“They’re so important for, you know, our ecosystem to be able to grow our submerged aquatic vegetation makes it really hard for fish to be able to do what they need to do. And other little critters and animals to be able to survive,” said Kistler.
The Corps disputes the characterization of the process as “mud dumping”
“I’ll be perfectly clear, actually. Mud dumping: we do not dump the mud into the mobile harbor. This is an estuary, which means that is a natural place where sediment flows from six river systems,” said Colonel Shaw.
Shaw said protecting the bay and maintaining the shipping channel are not mutually exclusive.
Daphne police search for stabbing suspect, victim recovering in ICU “Our people, they live here. They’re from here. They grew up here. They use the bay. They swim in the bay. They fish here. They eat the fish from here. They are part of the community. So, there’s. They are just as invested in making sure this bay stays healthy,” said Colonel Shaw.
